Volume 05 · Chapter 12

Behavioral economics and microeconomic evidence

Undergraduate Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v05-c11

By the endEvaluate departures from standard choice and the evidence needed to support interventions.

A behavioral explanation must make a discriminating prediction

Capability: evaluate departures from standard choice and the evidence needed to support interventions. Prerequisite: auctions, matching and market design, together with contingent strategies, hypothesis testing and causal identification. A default may change enrollment. An owner may demand more to sell an object than a nonowner offers to buy it. A person may purchase a restriction on tomorrow's choice. Each observation poses a question about preferences, beliefs, attention, constraints and the institution that elicited the choice.

Calling an outcome a “bias” does not answer that question. State a benchmark, a mechanism that departs from it, and an observation that could distinguish competing explanations. A choice can maximize a stable preference while reflecting scarce information, switching costs or a binding budget. Conversely, allowing a different unexplained preference for every observation makes a model difficult to test. This chapter develops two precise behavioral models and a complete small experimental analysis. Except for one explicitly dated replication-study summary, all numbers and data are original hypothetical constructions.

Reference dependence and loss aversion

A reference-independent consumer ranks final bundles using u(q,m), where q is an object's quantity and m is money. A reference-dependent consumer instead uses u(q,m;r), with r a reference quantity. Holding the feasible final bundles fixed, changing r can change their ranking. The reference could be an entitlement, an expectation or another comparison standard; a model must specify which and when it is set. An observed endowment and a psychological reference are not automatically the same variable.

Our deliberately small model has one indivisible object, q ∈ {0, 1}, and linear money utility. At the moment of choice, fix r ∈ {0, 1} and let

u(q,m;r) = m + v(q−r),   v(z) = az if z ≥ 0, and v(z) = λaz if z < 0,

where a > 0 is the gain value in USD per object and λ ≥ 1 is dimensionless. Money and v are measured in a common dollar utility scale. Loss aversion means λ > 1: losing a quantity relative to r lowers value more than gaining the same quantity raises it. Money itself has no separate loss-aversion kink in this example. Assume enough cash to finance every considered purchase, no transaction costs, no resale or information about quality conveyed by the offer, and a reference that remains fixed while alternatives are compared.

Loss aversion is distinct from diminishing sensitivity, which changes marginal value as the magnitude of a gain or loss increases. Our value function is linear on each side; its only nonlinearity is the kink at zero. Risk aversion is a preference for a sure expected payoff over a lottery. A kink can generate such a preference for a lottery crossing the reference, but risk aversion can also arise from smooth concave utility without reference dependence. A riskless buying–selling gap is not, by itself, a measurement of curvature or probability weighting. Full prospect theory contains additional ingredients not assumed here.

Tversky and Kahneman's 1991 Loss Aversion in Riskless Choice, section II, formalizes reference-indexed preferences and separates reference determination from its effect on choices. Its section III also discusses alternative sources of buying–selling discrepancies. We use an original one-object specialization, not a universal estimate of λ.

Worked example 1: buying, selling and changing the comparison point

Let a = 6 and λ = 2. A nonowner with reference r = 0 compares not buying, utility M, with buying at p, utility M−p+6. The largest acceptable price is therefore WTP = 6 USD, with indifference at equality. An owner with r = 1 compares keeping the object, utility M, with selling for p, utility M+p−12. The smallest acceptable sale price is WTA = 12 USD. Generally WTP = a and WTA = λa under these assumptions. At an offer of 8, the nonowner declines to buy and the owner declines to sell.

The income change from owning an object cannot explain this particular model's gap, because marginal utility of money is constant and affordability does not bind. If λ = 1, both thresholds equal 6. If λ rises while a stays fixed, WTA rises but WTP does not. These are conditional comparative predictions; adding loss aversion in money or changing reference formation would change the formulas.

We can isolate reference from the available final bundles mathematically. Offer a choice between X = (one object, zero dollars) and Y = (no object, eight dollars). At r = 0, their utilities are 6 and 8, so choose Y. At r = 1, their utilities are 0 and −4, so choose X. The bundles have not changed; the stipulated reference has. This is a framing prediction only if an intervention actually changes that reference without changing other relevant features.

A measured WTA/WTP ratio of two does not identify λ = 2 without the model. Budget constraints, different wealth, strategic bidding, misunderstanding, attachment from use, offer-dependent beliefs and transaction costs may create gaps. A useful design varies endowment or reference cues by random assignment, makes incentives and feasible exchanges clear, records wealth and experience, and tests alternative mechanisms. Randomizing a cue identifies the cue's effect on elicited choices; it does not automatically reveal an otherwise unobserved reference or a structural loss parameter.

Time consistency is about rankings across dates

Let us be a utility flow at date s, in a fixed common scale. Under exponential discounting, the date-t evaluation of a finite stream is Ut = Σs = tTδs−tus, with 0 < δ ≤ 1. Holding information, feasible continuation streams and utility functions fixed, the date-t ranking of streams that first differ after today is the date-(t+1) ranking multiplied by positive δ. Therefore the ranking cannot reverse merely because time passes. New information, changed constraints or state-dependent utility can rationally change a plan; this theorem does not hold those changes responsible for time inconsistency.

Quasi-hyperbolic discounting instead gives

Ut = ut + βΣs = t+1Tδs−tus,   0 < β ≤ 1.

When β < 1, all future utility is additionally downweighted relative to the present. Between two strictly future dates the relative weight is still δ per period; when the earlier date becomes today, its weight becomes one. This can reverse a ranking. β is present bias; δ captures exponential discounting among future periods. β = 1 restores the exponential model. A strong preference for an immediate payment alone cannot distinguish β, δ, liquidity need, payment risk or utility curvature.

David Laibson's 1997 Golden Eggs and Hyperbolic Discounting, section II, specifies these discount weights and models successive selves as players. Our finite action example uses that preference structure; it does not reproduce the paper's saving model or import its historical financial claims.

Worked example 2: a plan, a reversal and a priced commitment

There are three dates, 0, 1 and 2. At date 1 a person can perform a maintenance action costing c = 6 utility-equivalent USD immediately and producing a certain benefit b = 10 at date 2. Skipping produces zero at both dates. It cannot be performed on another date. There is no new information, liquidity problem, uncertainty or hidden change in tastes. Set β = 1/2 and δ = 1.

At date 0, the plan to perform the action has value (1/2)(−6+10) = 2, versus zero for skipping. At date 1, performing it has value −6+(1/2)10 = −1, versus zero for skipping. The date-1 self skips if free to choose. The preference reversal occurs although both selves correctly know the costs and benefits. More generally, the date-0 plan is strictly preferred when c < δb, while the date-1 self strictly skips when c > βδb. Thus a strict reversal requires βδb < c < δb. Equality at either boundary creates a tie, not a strict prediction.

At date 0, an optional device can instead make the date-1 action unavoidable at a fee k ≥ 0 paid immediately. Stipulate that the device is irreversible, understood and effective, with no other effects. The fee purchases a real service using resources worth k in the same scale; it is not merely a deposit returned later or a transfer whose recipient's gain has been omitted. This is a hypothetical feasible-set restriction, not a claim about the enforceability of a real contract.

A sophisticated person correctly anticipates the date-1 preference. Without commitment the action will be skipped and date-0 value is zero. With commitment date-0 value is 2−k. Commitment is strictly chosen for k < 2, rejected for k > 2, and tied with no commitment at k = 2. At k = 1 the person purchases it, performs the action and obtains date-0 value 1. The full contingent plan says that the date-1 self would skip if the device were not purchased. Backward reasoning, rather than the date-0 unconstrained plan alone, predicts behavior.

A fully naive person has the same actual β = 1/2 but predicts that tomorrow's self will act as if β̂ = 1. This person expects the desired action without commitment, so assigns no positive value to restricting the choice and rejects every k > 0. At date 1 the actual self nevertheless skips. At k = 0 commitment and no commitment are perceived as tied; no unique naive outcome follows without a tie rule. Naivety is a belief error about future choice, not a different actual discount factor. Partial awareness, β < β̂ < 1, is possible but is not estimated from this single case.

If the fee merely buys a reminder while skipping remains available and all stated payoffs remain unchanged, the date-1 choice is still to skip. An effective reminder would have to alter attention, information or another ingredient. If β = 1 at δ = 1, the date-1 self already performs the action, and commitment has no benefit at a positive fee. Observed demand for a restriction is suggestive only after alternative benefits such as insurance, convenience, better terms or information are ruled out.

Frank Schilbach's MIT 14.13 Time Preferences lectures, slides 40–51 and 61, distinguish β from beliefs β̂ and explain backward reasoning for sophisticated selves. The notes credit earlier materials by Kőszegi and Laibson and the naivety/sophistication framework of O'Donoghue and Rabin. The costs, benefits and fee calculations here are original.

Which welfare criterion evaluates an intervention?

Decision utility describes the ranking that produces a choice in its decision context. Experienced utility concerns the well-being flows during outcomes. Neither is directly observed merely by seeing a click, an enrollment or a purchase. A welfare analysis must specify which flows count, their measurement, whose preferences or reports inform them, and how they are aggregated across dates and people.

In the maintenance example at k = 1, the date-0 criterion favors commitment by 1. An undiscounted flow criterion W = −k−c+b favors it by 3. At date 1, once the fee is sunk, the person would prefer release: the remaining action has date-1 value −1 rather than zero. Thus commitment is not an improvement according to every temporal self. At k = 3, W still rises by 1, but date-0 utility falls by 1, so the sophisticated person declines. Selecting W rather than U₀ is a normative choice, not an algebraic implication of present bias.

Other possible criteria include choices made after accurate information and deliberation in a stable context, a specified long-run preference, or an explicitly measured well-being index. Explain why that criterion is appropriate and examine sensitivity to it. Reference-dependent losses may themselves be experienced harms; an analyst cannot simply erase them by labeling them irrational. Voluntary informed commitment gives evidence about the earlier self's ranking, but does not prove that every future self benefits or that compulsory commitment is warranted.

Heterogeneity and resources matter. If c = 6, k = 1 but another person's benefit is only b = 4, compulsory commitment gives W = −3; the first person's b = 10 gives W = 3. A population with equal shares has zero average W change before any further administrative cost. The informed low-benefit person would reject voluntary commitment. Distribution, accurate beliefs, ability to opt out, reversibility after unforeseen events, privacy and implementation costs can change a policy comparison. A positive effect on an intermediate behavior is insufficient to sign welfare.

Attention and defaults: the mechanism is part of the hypothesis

A default is the option implemented if no active change is made. It can affect choices because people overlook an alternative, face an action cost, infer advice from the chosen default, or value retaining a reference position. Those are different mechanisms. A default need not benefit everyone, and choosing it need not reveal a preference for its consequences under full attention and costless switching.

For a small attention model, suppose an alternative has known net benefit B > 0 if considered. It is noticed with probability a, and adopted whenever noticed; otherwise the default remains. Adoption probability is then a. A reminder that changes a from 2/5 to 4/5 raises adoption by 2/5 in this stipulated model. The same aggregate rates can arise with full attention if switching-cost distributions put 2/5 and 4/5 of people below B in the two environments. The adoption contrast alone does not tell those mechanisms apart. Attention checks, directly measured action costs, neutral information and independently varied defaults can yield discriminating evidence; conditioning on a post-treatment attention measure does not automatically identify a mediated effect.

Likewise, apparent overconfidence requires a forecast and a scoring benchmark, not just a bad realized outcome. A well-calibrated forecaster will sometimes be wrong. A framing hypothesis should hold objective consequences, probabilities and feasible options fixed, or explicitly model the information conveyed by the wording. These examples explain how to formulate behavioral questions without treating a catalogue of labels as a theory.

Experiments identify the intervention that was actually assigned

A laboratory experiment can control payoffs and information closely; a field experiment embeds assignment in a natural decision environment. Neither label guarantees valid implementation, representative sampling or a welfare-relevant outcome. Define the unit, target population, assignment law, intervention, outcome window and measurement before inspecting results. Random assignment justifies comparisons within the experimental population; random sampling is a separate route to population representativeness.

Use Zi for assignment and Yi(z) for a person's completion outcome under each assigned interface. With a well-defined treatment and no interference, Yi = ZiYi(1)+(1−Zi)Yi(0). The finite-population assignment effect is τ = (1/N)Σ[Yi(1)−Yi(0)]. Calling the mean difference an intention-to-treat effect keeps people in their assigned groups even if they ignore the interface or do not activate the suggested option. Comparing voluntary users with nonusers answers a different, generally selected comparison.

Worked example 3: a large observed contrast with an exact small experiment

Eight hypothetical eligible people see an interface for booking a voluntary learning session. On relative day 0, a lottery selects exactly four people uniformly among all C(8, 4) = 70 subsets. Z = 1 receives a preselected booking option; Z = 0 receives the same option initially unselected. Both can change the choice, with the same stated prices and information. Y = 1 means the person completes the session by the end of day 7. Every outcome is observed by the same rule, assignment is delivered as specified, and people do not affect one another's outcomes. These are synthetic data, not a report of a conducted experiment.

Assigned interface and observed completion in the original synthetic case
PersonP01P02P03P04P05P06P07P08
Z11110000
Y11111000

The treatment completion rate is 4/4 = 1 and the control rate is 1/4. The observed difference T is 3/4, or 75 percentage points, not a 75% relative increase. The corresponding relative increase over the control rate would be 300%, a different statistic. The prespecified analysis uses the difference in rates and a two-sided test based on |T|.

Test the sharp null H₀: Yi(1) = Yi(0) for every person. Under this null, each observed outcome is the person's outcome under either assignment, so hold the five ones and three zeros fixed and enumerate the 70 allowed treatment subsets. If K of the five completers are assigned treatment, T = K/4−(5−K)/4 = (2K−5)/4. Count subsets by selecting K completers and 4−K noncompleters:

Exact assignment distribution under the sharp null
KTNumber C(5,K)C(3, 4−K)
1−3/45
2−1/430
31/430
43/45

Exactly ten assignments have |T| ≥ 3/4, so the inclusive two-sided p-value is 10/70 = 1/7 ≈ 0.143. Do not reject at the prespecified 5% level. This does not establish zero effect, negligible effect or a 1/7 probability that H₀ is true. The null concerns every individual effect, which is stronger than an average effect of zero. A sharp-null test is not automatically a test or confidence interval for an arbitrary heterogeneous average effect.

The tail test is valid because, under H₀, the actual assignment is uniform over the same 70 possibilities used in the calculation. For any significance threshold α, the assignments whose inclusive upper-tail ranks are at most 70α number at most 70α; ties can only make the rule conservative. Thus its rejection probability is at most α. No iid Bernoulli assumption for the assignment indicators is needed: their sum is fixed at four. A clustered or blocked lottery would require its own allowed assignments.

The causal contrast estimates the effect of the assigned interface on completion in these eight people. Even if precisely estimated, it would not separate attention from action costs, endorsement beliefs or reference effects, nor establish the benefit of completing the session. It also would not identify an effect in a new population without a transport argument.

Peng Ding's A First Course in Causal Inference, 3 October 2023 preprint, sections 3.1–3.3, defines complete randomization and the sharp-null randomization test. The enumeration and rank argument above are developed for this original case. Identification and confounding supplies the finite-population unbiasedness proof.

A synthetic counterfactual audit is different from an empirical estimate

For an instructor-only check, stipulate potential outcomes Y(0) = (0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0) and Y(1) = (1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 0). They generate the observed table at the displayed assignment. Four people have effect one, so the true synthetic τ is 1/2. Averaging the observed mean differences across all 70 reassignments, now recomputing each person's outcome under the assignment, gives exactly 1/2 and assignment variance 1/16. This is a sampling-distribution calculation under a supplied effect schedule. It is not the sharp-null test, which holds the observed outcome vector fixed.

Another compatible schedule sets both potential outcomes equal to the observed Y for each person. Its τ is zero and it produces the same displayed observations. Actual experiments do not reveal both potential outcomes. The lottery makes the difference unbiased across assignments; it does not make the missing counterfactuals visible in one realization. The two analyses use different premises and answer different questions.

Download the synthetic input, standard-library enumeration program, preserved output and README into one directory. Run python3 v05-c12-randomization.py. The observed-only test does not consult the separate synthetic oracle. All 70 assignments are enumerated, so there is no Monte Carlo error or seed choice. The program uses no network or third-party package.

Threats to interpretation and an auditable analysis plan

Attrition: randomization does not randomize who remains observed after treatment. Record missing outcomes and their reasons by assignment; do not code an unknown completion as zero without a justified rule. With a bounded outcome, show how worst-case missing values affect the contrast. Equal attrition rates alone do not prove the retained groups comparable. Noncompliance: retain assignment for the intention-to-treat comparison. An effect of receipt needs further assumptions and methods; selecting recipients or controlling for a post-treatment choice does not supply them.

Measurement and demand effects: a participant may respond to what they infer the researcher wants, while an assessor may score outcomes differently after learning assignment. Fix outcome definitions and timing, use consistent records, and blind measurement where feasible. If treatment changes reporting as well as behavior, the measured effect combines those channels. Spillovers require an appropriate unit and exposure model, often with assignment at a group level.

Multiple testing and flexibility: choosing among outcomes, subgroups, directions, stopping dates and exclusions after seeing results changes the inference problem. Prespecify the primary outcome, estimand, assignment-based test, missingness rule, multiplicity adjustment and stopping rule. Timestamp a preregistration before outcome access, preserve later amendments, and label exploratory analyses. Preregistration cannot fix poor measurement, an ineffective intervention or inadequate precision; a plan is useful because it makes choices inspectable.

External validity: report eligibility, recruitment, incentives, implementation, stakes and context. A tightly controlled laboratory result may reveal a mechanism under those conditions; field recruitment can still be selective. A different default, population, follow-up horizon or institution may change both compliance and welfare. A theory plus transparent comparison of effect modifiers can support transfer, but random assignment within one sample is not random sampling of all settings.

Reproducibility, replication and learning from disagreement

We use computational reproducibility for obtaining the stated result from the same inputs and procedure, and replication for studying the claim with new observations under an explicitly documented design. Terminology differs across fields, so state the operation. Re-running this chapter's program is reproducibility. Recruiting a new sample and executing its assignment protocol would be a replication; changing defaults or institutions would additionally test generalizability. A successful re-run cannot validate random assignment, a psychological mechanism or the original measurements.

A bounded historical example illustrates why the criterion matters. Camerer and colleagues' 2016 economics replication project studied 18 results from articles published in the American Economic Review and Quarterly Journal of Economics during 2011–2014. Its author-deposited abstract reports that 11 replications produced a statistically significant estimate with the original sign, and that other assessment criteria gave different rates. That is evidence about those selected results under stated criteria, not a failure probability for all economics or all behavioral hypotheses. We have not independently reanalyzed those data.

A replication report should compare effect estimates, units and uncertainty, not only whether each p-value crosses 0.05. Explain changes in sample, protocol, treatment delivery, outcomes and analysis. Distinguish a coding discrepancy from sampling variation, a weak manipulation, a context-dependent effect or a failed mechanism. Preserve raw inputs, provenance, code, software versions, analysis decisions and a discrepancy log as in empirical integration and replication. An intervention recommendation then needs an additional welfare and implementation argument; reproducible significance alone is insufficient.

Exercises

  1. In the one-object model set a = 8 and λ = 3/2. Derive WTP and WTA from the utility comparisons, state choices at a price of 10, and show the effect of λ = 1. For the fixed alternatives X = (1, 0), Y = (0, 10), compare r = 0 and r = 1. Name two assumptions needed before treating an observed ratio WTA/WTP as an estimate of λ.
  2. Consider a separate monetary value function w(x) = x for x ≥ 0 and w(x) = 2x for x < 0, with a fixed reference at zero and ordinary probability averaging. Compare a sure zero with equal chances of +2 and −2. Then compare a sure 4 with equal chances of 2 and 6. Explain precisely what these comparisons do and do not show about loss aversion, risk aversion and curvature.
  3. Prove the strict reversal condition βδb < c < δb for the three-date action. Set c = 7, b = 12, β = 1/2, δ = 9/10. Calculate the date-0 plan value, date-1 action value and highest weakly acceptable immediate commitment fee for a sophisticated person. Give naive and sophisticated choices at a fee of 1. Repeat the behavior comparison for β = 1, keeping δ fixed, and discuss equality cases.
  4. For the baseline c = 6, b = 10, β = 1/2, δ = 1 example, compare no commitment with effective commitment at k = 1 and k = 3 under U₀, undiscounted W and date-1 continuation utility after the fee is sunk. Is either comparison a Pareto improvement for all temporal selves? Then apply compulsory k = 1 commitment to equal shares of people with b = 10 and b = 4. Calculate the average W change and explain why informed voluntary take-up would differ.
  5. Reconstruct the complete sharp-null distribution for the eight-person experiment using counts of selected completers. Compute the observed contrast and inclusive two-sided p-value. If a one-sided positive-direction test had genuinely been specified in advance, what would its p-value be? State why selecting that direction after seeing the data is different and why neither test directly tests only τ = 0.
  6. For the supplied synthetic potential outcomes, compute every individual effect and the true average. Prove that complete-randomization mean differences average to τ without assuming independent assignments across people. Explain why the null test's fixed-outcome enumeration cannot be substituted for this calculation. Without using the oracle, derive the logical minimum and maximum finite-population τ compatible with the observed binary table; distinguish that range from a confidence interval.
  7. Suppose outcomes for treated P03 and P04 are now missing; treated P01 and P02 are observed completers and the original four control outcomes remain observed. Find the range of the full assigned-group completion contrast compatible with the missing binary outcomes, and the complete-case contrast. Why need the latter not estimate the original intention-to-treat effect? If some people also ignore or reverse their assigned default, explain why comparing actual adopters with nonadopters does not preserve randomization.
  8. A researcher tests five independent true nulls at 0.05 and reports only a favorable result. Calculate the probability of at least one false rejection. For five planned tests with p-values 0.008, 0.02, 0.04, 0.30, 0.70, compare individual 0.05 decisions with Bonferroni control at family level 0.05. Design a concise confirmatory replication of the default intervention: specify the target, design, measurement, analysis and welfare evidence. Explain why successfully rerunning the original code and the historical ratio 11/18 cannot by themselves validate a new policy.
Complete solutions and evaluation criteria

  1. A nonowner buys if M−p+8 ≥ M, so WTP = 8. An owner sells if M+p−(3/2)8 ≥ M, so WTA = 12. At p = 10 the nonowner declines and the owner keeps the object. With λ = 1 both thresholds are 8; then the nonowner still declines at 10 and the owner sells. For the fixed bundles at r = 0, values are 8 and 10, so choose Y; at r = 1 they are 0 and 10−12 = −2, so choose X. The observed ratio identifies λ only within assumptions such as linear money utility without binding affordability, known fixed references, no relevant transaction costs or strategic misreporting, and the same underlying a. Naming two with their role is sufficient; a bare claim that randomization proves a psychological parameter is not.

  2. The crossing-reference lottery has value (1/2)2+(1/2)(−4) = −1, below sure zero, although both have monetary mean zero. This is risk-averse behavior for that lottery generated by the loss-aversion kink. The all-gain lottery has value (1/2)2+(1/2)6 = 4, equal to sure 4, so the person is neutral for this comparison. There is no smooth curvature within either domain. The function is globally concave because its slope falls from 2 to 1 at zero, so it produces weak risk aversion under ordinary probability averaging, with strictness for relevant crossing lotteries. Loss aversion describes the gain/loss asymmetry; it is not the general definition of risk aversion, and a smooth concave reference-independent utility could also reject the first lottery.

  3. At date 0 the action stream relative to skipping is βδ(−c+δb), positive exactly when c < δb because βδ > 0. At date 1 it is −c+βδb, negative exactly when c > βδb. Their conjunction gives the stated strict interval. For the new numbers, δb = 54/5 = 10.8 and βδb = 27/5 = 5.4, placing c = 7 inside it. Date 0 value is (9/20)(19/5) = 171/100 = 1.71; date 1 value is −8/5 = −1.6. With skipping predicted absent commitment, the highest weakly acceptable immediate fee is 1.71. The sophisticated person buys at 1; the fully naive person predicts action without commitment, refuses that fee, and actually skips later.

    At β = 1, the date 1 value is 19/5 > 0 and the date 0 value is 171/50 = 3.42. Both naive and sophisticated descriptions now predict the same future action, so no positive commitment fee is worthwhile solely for forcing it. At c = βδb the acting self is indifferent; at c = δb the earlier plan is tied. Actual outcomes at those boundaries need a tie rule, and the maximum fee must be recalculated from the selected no-commitment continuation. At the baseline fee threshold itself, commitment and no commitment are both optimal for the sophisticated date 0 self.

  4. Without commitment, actual skipping yields U₀ = W = 0 and continuation utility 0. At k = 1, commitment yields U₀ = −1+(1/2)(−6+10) = 1, W = −1−6+10 = 3 and date 1 continuation value −6+5 = −1. At k = 3 these are −1, 1 and −1. The paid fee is absent from the date 1 incremental comparison because it is sunk in both continuation alternatives. The date 1 self would prefer release in either case, so neither committed stream dominates skipping for every temporal self. Date 0 voluntarily chooses k = 1 but refuses k = 3, even though W favors both.

    With compulsory k = 1, people with b = 10 gain 3 under W, and people with b = 4 lose 3. Equal shares average zero before extra administrative costs; calling only the favorable group's benefit “the policy effect” would omit harms. Informed people with b = 4 value commitment at −1+(1/2)(−6+4) = −2 at date 0 and decline. Voluntary take-up therefore differs from universal assignment under the stated information and preferences.

  5. There are five completers and three noncompleters. K can be 1, 2, 3 or 4, with counts C(5,K)C(3, 4−K) = 5, 30, 30, 5. The corresponding differences are −3/4, −1/4, 1/4, 3/4. The observed K = 4 gives 3/4. Two-sided tail count 10 gives p = 1/7; the prespecified positive tail would count only K = 4, giving 5/70 = 1/14, still above 0.05. Choosing the favorable direction after observation does not implement that prespecified one-sided rule and invalidates its claimed error interpretation. Fixing outcomes across assignments is justified by zero effect for every unit. A zero average with offsetting individual effects does not fix those outcomes, so this sharp-null test is not automatically a valid test of that weaker composite null.

  6. The effects are (1, 1, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 0), averaging 4/8 = 1/2. Each person has treatment probability 4/8. Hence E[(1/4)ΣZᵢYᵢ(1)] = (1/8)ΣYᵢ(1), and the analogous control expectation is (1/8)ΣYᵢ(0). Subtracting gives τ; linearity of expectation does not require the Zᵢ to be independent. Reassignment under this oracle must change observed outcomes to the appropriate Yᵢ(z). The sharp-null enumeration instead assumes the two potential outcomes are equal and keeps the displayed outcomes fixed. It has mean-zero contrasts under its null, not the oracle's mean 1/2.

    For each of the four treated completers, the missing Y(0) is 0 or 1, so each effect is 0 or 1. Their total contribution lies in [0, 4]. The control completer can have effect −1 or 0; each of the three control noncompleters can have effect 0 or 1. Their total lies in [−1, 3]. Therefore the compatible τ range is [−1/8, 7/8], and both endpoints can be attained by choosing the missing binary values accordingly. This is a logical compatibility range for one observed table, not a 95% confidence interval derived from assignment probabilities. The all-zero-effect schedule is also compatible, while the supplied oracle provides another compatible schedule with τ = 1/2.

  7. The treated completion count lies between 2 and 4, so its full-group rate lies in [1/2, 1]. The control rate is 1/4, giving a contrast in [1/4, 3/4]. Complete cases instead give 2/2−1/4 = 3/4, the upper endpoint. The original randomization covers all eight people, not the subgroup whose outcomes happen to remain observed. Missingness could select treated noncompleters, so the complete-case contrast need not have the original unbiasedness property. A valid analysis reports the missingness, uses justified assumptions or bounds, and does not quietly replace unknown outcomes by failures. Default adoption is also a choice after assignment, potentially related to motivation and potential completion. Keep assigned groups for the assignment effect; a causal receipt effect needs an additional design or identification argument.

  8. Under independence, the probability of at least one false rejection is 1−0.95⁵ = 0.2262190625, about 22.6%. Individual tests reject the first three supplied p-values. Bonferroni compares each to 0.05/5 = 0.01 and rejects only 0.008; its family error guarantee does not require independence when each p-value is valid.

    A strong replication plan defines eligible people and the population target; randomly assigns a fully specified default with a recorded allocation law and suitable interference unit; uses the same fixed completion window and consistent measurement; plans sample size for a substantively relevant contrast; and timestamps the primary assignment-effect estimator, test direction, multiplicity, stopping and missingness procedures before outcomes are inspected. It records adoption without substituting an adopter comparison for randomization, documents recruitment and implementation differences, and reports effects and uncertainty whether or not significant. Welfare evidence should measure benefits, time/resource costs and harms, including heterogeneity and the value of opting out, under a stated criterion. Other defensible designs receive credit when their assignment and estimand match.

    Re-running original code checks same-data reproducibility, not new-data replication or causal assumptions. The historical 11/18 ≈ 61.1% describes one set of selected published results and one success criterion, not a probability that a new default policy helps. Policy support needs relevant evidence and a welfare/implementation argument for its own context.

Teach-back and Delayed check

Teach-back: explain why a choice reversal, a randomized behavior effect and a welfare improvement are three different claims. State the parameter and comparison in each behavioral model, reproduce the 70-assignment test's logic, and give one alternative mechanism. A complete answer specifies reference/timing, counterfactuals, uncertainty and whose welfare criterion is being used.

Delayed check: take a = 10, λ = 3/2 in the one-object model; then take c = 5, b = 9, β = 1/2, δ = 1 in the three-date action. Give the valuation thresholds, both date-specific action values and the sophisticated commitment-fee threshold. Finally, in a new complete lottery assigning three of six people, suppose all three treated people complete and all three controls do not. Derive the two-sided sharp-null p-value and interpret it at 5%.

Delayed-check answers

WTP = 10 and WTA = 15. The date 0 action value is (1/2)(−5+9) = 2, while date 1 value is −5+(1/2)9 = −1/2, so an unrestricted later self skips. A sophisticated person weakly accepts commitment fees up to 2, with a tie at 2. In the new experiment there are C(6, 3) = 20 assignments; only assigning all three completers or all three noncompleters to treatment produces |T| ≥ 1. Hence p = 2/20 = 1/10. Do not reject at 5%; a rate difference of 100 percentage points with such a small sample still does not establish a precise effect or imply that the null has 90% probability.

Next: apply the volume's models and evidence standards in the Volume 5 assessment and project package. Complete its examinations, reproducible project and delayed transfer before advancing. Macroeconomics and the international economy extends the analysis to aggregate activity and institutions.

Sources and further study

  • Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman — Loss Aversion in Riskless Choice: A Reference-Dependent Model (1991) — Reference-indexed preferences, loss aversion versus diminishing sensitivity, and alternative explanations of buying/selling discrepancies; original one-object specialization in this chapter.
  • David Laibson — Golden Eggs and Hyperbolic Discounting (1997) — Quasi-hyperbolic weights and temporal-self reasoning; the chapter supplies a distinct finite action/commitment model.
  • Frank Schilbach — MIT 14.13, Lectures 3 and 4: Time Preferences (Theory), 10 and 12 February 2020 — Actual present bias versus beliefs about future selves; naive/sophisticated behavior, commitment and backward reasoning.
  • Peng Ding — A First Course in Causal Inference, version 2 preprint, 3 October 2023 — Complete randomized assignment, individual sharp null, exact inclusive randomization p-value and difference-in-means statistic.
  • Colin F. Camerer and colleagues — Evaluating replicability of laboratory experiments in economics (Science, 2016) — Precisely bounded historical example: 18 selected AER/QJE results from 2011–2014 and 11 replications significant with original sign; success criterion matters.
